title: Daruka, the Last Messenger
story:
After the slaughter at Prabhasa, the survivors searched for Balarama. Krishna walked out of the ruin with his charioteer Daruka and with Vabhru, following the trail of the man who had walked away from everything. He had left the carnage without a word, and the three of them followed the silence he left behind. They found him at last in a solitary spot, sitting with his back against a tree, thoughtful, his great arms folded, looking at nothing. The man who had levelled armies with his plough-arm sat as still as the tree, as though the strength had gone out of him with his clan.

Krishna stood before his brother and gave his orders, and there was no collapse in his voice, only care. "Daruka," he said, "go to the Kurus. Inform Partha of this great slaughter of the Yadus. Let Arjuna come here quickly, hearing of the destruction of the Yadavas through the brahmin's curse."

Daruka, deprived of his senses by grief, climbed onto his car and drove toward Hastinapura without looking back, carrying the worst news a messenger had ever carried. The road to the Kurus was long, and the news would not keep.

Then Krishna turned to Vabhru, the last of the heroes left standing beside him. "Go quickly," he said, "and protect the ladies. Let no robbers do them any injury, tempted by the wealth that is with them." Vabhru, still helpless with wine and cheerless at the slaughter of his kinsmen, touched his hand and departed. He had rested for a while by Krishna's side, but as soon as he had gone a little distance, the iron bolt found him. It attached itself to a mallet in the hands of a hunter, and of its own accord it sprang upon that solitary survivor of the Yadava race and slew him. He too had been named in the curse of the brahmins. The bolt had been ground to powder and scattered on the sea, and yet it had kept its shape somewhere, waiting for a hunter's hand.

Krishna saw it happen and did not move. He, who was fully acquainted with the end of all things, had known the bolt would not stay buried. He turned to Balarama. "Wait for me here," he said, "till I place the ladies under the care of kinsmen."

He entered the city of Dwaravati and went to his father. "Protect all the ladies of our house," he said, "till Dhananjaya comes. At the skirts of the forest Rama is waiting for me. I shall meet him today. This great carnage of the Yadus I have beheld, even as I beheld the carnage of the foremost Kshatriyas of Kuru's race. It is impossible for me to see this city of the Yadavas without the Yadavas beside me. Know that, proceeding to the woods, I shall practise penances with Rama in my company."

He touched his father's feet with his head and quickly left his presence.

Behind him the wailing began, the women of the house and the children crying out together, a sound like the city tearing in two. Krishna stopped, retraced his footsteps, and stood before them. "Arjuna will come here," he said. "That foremost of men will relieve you of your grief."

Then he walked out of Dwaraka toward the forest where his brother waited, and the city was left holding its breath, watching the yellow cloth of his robe grow small against the trees. No one at the gate moved until the cloth had vanished into the green, and then the wailing began again, softer this time, as if the city no longer had the heart for it.
reflection: Krishna's last commands are all acts of care: a messenger sent to the one man in the world who could guard the women, a promise spoken to the weeping household. Even at the edge of his own ending, he arranges the world's protection first — and the telling lets the reader watch him walk away knowing he will not come back.
content_note: Contains the sudden death of Vabhru and the sorrowful atmosphere of the Yadava race's final hours; best shared with older children or with an adult to give context.
next_story_tease: Arjuna would hear the news soon enough, and carry it home to Hastinapura.
hero_scene: Krishna, in yellow robes, walking out of the city of Dwaraka toward the forest where Balarama waits, while behind him the women and children of his house wail at the gate.
